content: Ovalbumin is the predominant protein found in egg white, accounting for approximately 60-65% of the total protein content. It is classified as a member of the serpin superfamily of proteins. However, unlike most serpins, ovalbumin does not possess the ability to inhibit proteases. The precise biological function of ovalbumin remains unclear, but it is hypothesized to serve as a storage protein. Ovalbumin plays a significant role in various fields of scientific research. It is widely used in studies of protein structure and properties due to its abundance and availability. In the context of serpin research, ovalbumin's inability to inhibit proteases provides a unique opportunity to compare its structure with that of inhibitory serpins, thereby identifying the structural features necessary for protease inhibition. In proteomics, chicken egg ovalbumin is frequently employed as a molecular weight marker for calibrating electrophoresis gels. Additionally, in immunological studies, ovalbumin is commonly used to induce allergic reactions in experimental models. The ovalbumin protein derived from chickens consists of 385 amino acids and has a relative molecular mass of 45 kilodaltons (kD). It is a glycoprotein with four glycosylation sites. Despite lacking an N-terminal leader sequence, ovalbumin is secreted from the cell. From a medicinal perspective, ovalbumin has potential therapeutic applications in cases of heavy metal poisoning, such as iron toxicity. Ovalbumin has the ability to chelate heavy metals, binding the metal ions through its sulfhydryl bonds. This chelation process prevents the absorption of the metals into the gastrointestinal tract, thereby mitigating the risk of poisoning.
